paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems built from several terms that require different computational tools. One term is smooth and provides a gradient, while other terms may be nonsmooth but provide proximal operators. Three operator splitting combines these tools to solve the overall problem. The authors introduce a version that adapts its step size using local information about the objective.

The practical motivation is to take larger steps when the objective permits them while retaining the original method’s convergence properties. The adaptation requires two additional function evaluations per iteration and only an initial step size estimate, without further step size hyperparameters. This gives the algorithm a way to respond to the problem during optimization.

The analysis establishes sublinear convergence for general convex objectives and linear convergence under stronger assumptions. These rates match the best known rates for the nonadaptive version. Comparisons across six problems illustrate a computational advantage, supporting adaptation as a practical improvement without claiming a universally faster convergence rate.
icml-2018-adaptive-three-operator-splitt.tldr: Adaptive step sizes make three operator splitting more computationally effective in experiments while preserving established convergence rates.

paragraphs: A source sentence can have several valid translations, so uncertainty is part of the translation task itself. Noisy training examples add another source of uncertainty. This paper examines how these two sources relate to familiar problems in neural translation, including worse performance with larger search beams, underestimated rare words, and limited diversity among generated translations.

The authors develop tools and metrics for examining how a model distributes probability across possible translations and how that distribution interacts with search. Their results indicate that search performs remarkably well, while the models tend to disperse too much probability across the space of candidate outputs. This finding directs attention toward the learned distribution when diagnosing translation problems.

The study also introduces tools for assessing calibration: whether the model’s confidence appropriately reflects its behavior. The authors show ways to correct some calibration shortcomings and release code alongside multiple human translations for two benchmarks. Together, these contributions make uncertainty something that can be examined directly when evaluating both translation models and their decoding procedures.
icml-2018-analyzing-uncertainty-in-neura.tldr: The study links translation problems to uncertainty and finds that models spread probability too broadly even when search works well.

paragraphs: Generative models need to produce convincing outputs while preserving the variety present in the distribution they learn. This paper introduces autoregressive implicit quantile networks, or AIQN, which capture a distribution through quantile regression. The central change is the way the model represents and learns that distribution, offering a different approach to generative modeling.

The method is designed to fit into many existing models and architectures. The authors demonstrate it by extending PixelCNN and evaluating image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Their evaluation combines Inception scores and FID with samples that were not selectively chosen and image inpainting results. These provide several perspectives on the resulting images rather than relying on a single assessment.

Across the reported observations, AIQN improves perceptual quality and evaluation metrics while retaining sample diversity. The authors also consistently observe stable algorithmic behavior. The significance is that the reported quality gains do not come with a corresponding loss of variety: the learned distribution continues to support a diverse collection of outputs.
icml-2018-autoregressive-quantile-networ.tldr: AIQN uses quantile regression for generative modeling and improves reported image quality while maintaining diversity and stable learning.

paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, a player repeatedly chooses among actions and learns from their rewards. This paper considers feedback that is especially difficult to interpret: rewards arrive after random delays, and each round reveals only the sum of whichever rewards arrive then. The player loses the connection between an individual reward and the action that generated it.

The authors ask how much this lost information increases regret, the performance cost of learning which actions to choose. Earlier results for delayed feedback that retained action identities found an additive cost related to expected delay. The paper shows that an additive increase remains possible with anonymous, aggregated feedback when the expected delay, or a bound on it, is known.

The proposed algorithm exactly matches the nonanonymous problem’s worst case regret when delays are bounded. With unbounded delays, the match holds up to logarithmic factors or an additional variance term. These distinctions show how the guarantees depend on delay behavior despite the extra difficulty of assigning credit.
icml-2018-bandits-with-delayed-aggregate.tldr: With known expected delay information, anonymous aggregated bandit feedback can retain additive delay costs in regret.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression provides a distribution over predictions, making uncertainty a central part of its output. Improvements in inducing point methods had accelerated marginal likelihood calculations and posterior means, but estimating posterior covariance and drawing samples remained expensive. This paper targets those remaining operations, which are needed to work with the predictive distribution beyond its mean.

The proposed method, LOVE, uses the Lanczos algorithm to approximate the predictive covariance matrix efficiently. Covariance describes how uncertainty in different predictions varies together, so accelerating its calculation supports a richer predictive output. The authors report substantial improvements in both time and memory complexity through this approximation approach.

In their experiments, covariance calculations are up to 2,000 times faster and sample generation is 18,000 times faster than existing methods, without observed loss of accuracy. These are reported experimental speedups. The contribution is to make distributional prediction and sampling more computationally accessible, extending efficiency improvements to the uncertainty calculations that remained bottlenecks.
icml-2018-constant-time-predictive-distr.tldr: LOVE approximates Gaussian process predictive covariance with Lanczos, delivering large experimental speedups for covariance estimation and sampling.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to remove noise from discrete-time signals using a family of adaptive convolution estimators. Each estimator uses a time-invariant filter, but the filter itself is learned from the data by solving a convex optimization problem. The overall estimator can therefore be nonlinear even though the resulting filter is time-invariant.

Previous work had established favorable statistical properties for these estimators. The authors focus on making them computationally efficient, implementing them with established first-order proximal algorithms. This connects an estimator family with statistical appeal to optimization procedures that can carry out the required fitting. The contribution concerns how to compute the estimators efficiently, rather than introducing their statistical motivation.

The paper also analyzes computational complexity in relation to statistical accuracy. This ties the effort spent solving the optimization problem to the accuracy relevant for estimating a noisy signal. A simulated benchmark illustrates both the proposed procedures and their analysis, bringing the computational and statistical aspects of denoising into the same account.
icml-2018-efficient-first-order-algorith.tldr: The paper makes adaptive convolution denoisers efficient to compute and analyzes their cost in terms of statistical accuracy.

paragraphs: Efficient Neural Architecture Search, or ENAS, reduces the computational cost of automatically designing neural networks. It places candidate architectures inside one large computational graph, with each candidate represented by a subgraph. Because these subgraphs share parameters, the search can reuse learned weights across different candidate designs.

A controller learns through policy gradient to select subgraphs that maximize expected reward on validation data. Meanwhile, the model associated with a selected subgraph is trained using cross entropy. This couples architecture selection with shared model training: the controller explores designs while parameter sharing reduces the GPU time required to support that exploration.

The authors report a search cost 1,000 times lower than standard Neural Architecture Search alongside strong predictive results. On Penn Treebank, the discovered architecture reaches test perplexity of 56.3, comparable to leading methods without post-training processing. On CIFAR-10, its 2.89% test error is described as comparable to NASNet’s 2.65%. These results support parameter sharing as an effective way to make architecture search substantially cheaper.
icml-2018-efficient-neural-architecture-.tldr: ENAS shares weights across candidate architectures to greatly reduce search cost while finding models with competitive performance.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to support vector classification with more than two classes. Multicategory SVM has a natural interpretation as an extension of binary SVM, but computational difficulties have limited its use. Simplex-cone SVM is computationally efficient, while its interpretation has appeared less transparent. The authors establish that the two formulations are exactly equivalent.

They also provide a one-to-one correspondence between the methods’ tuning parameters. This makes the equivalence operational: choices in one formulation can be translated into the other. As a result, the multicategory SVM interpretation can be paired with the efficient computation associated with simplex-cone SVM, bringing together advantages previously viewed as belonging to separate methods.

The paper additionally develops a Donsker theorem for finite-dimensional kernel multicategory SVM and an asymptotic covariance formula. This statistical analysis partially explains why One-vs-Rest methods can compete strongly with multicategory SVM. Using the covariance result, the authors construct an inverse-variance weighted classification rule that improves on the One-vs-Rest approach.
icml-2018-equivalence-of-multicategory-s.tldr: An exact equivalence links interpretable multicategory SVMs to efficient simplex-cone computation and supports a new variance-weighted classifier.

paragraphs: A prediction interval expresses uncertainty in a regression output by giving a range of plausible values. This paper starts from a direct quality criterion: intervals should be narrow while still containing a specified fraction of the data. The two requirements belong together, because reducing width alone does not establish that an interval adequately represents uncertainty.

The authors derive a neural network loss from this criterion without requiring a distributional assumption. They connect the loss to a likelihood principle and show that it can be optimized with gradient descent. This makes interval quality part of the training objective, directly linking what the network learns to the desired combination of width and coverage.

The approach also uses an ensemble to account for model uncertainty. In benchmark experiments, the authors report improvements over leading uncertainty quantification methods, including a reduction of more than 10% in average interval width. The result supports training explicitly for useful intervals while incorporating uncertainty associated with the model itself.
icml-2018-high-quality-prediction-interv.tldr: A distribution-free training loss and ensemble produce prediction intervals with over 10% lower average width in reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: The Image Transformer adapts a self-attention architecture to image generation formulated as a sequence modeling problem. Its autoregressive formulation provides a tractable likelihood, allowing the model to assign an evaluable probability to an image. The work extends an architecture used for textual sequences to the dependencies involved in generating images.

The main practical adjustment restricts attention to local neighborhoods. This lets the model process substantially larger images while still giving each layer a larger receptive field than typical convolutional networks. The approach therefore uses local attention to balance the amount of image context available to a layer with the computational demands of processing that context.

On ImageNet, the authors improve the best published negative log-likelihood from 3.83 to 3.77. They also apply an encoder-decoder version to image super-resolution with a large magnification ratio. In a human evaluation, its outputs fool observers three times as often as the previous leading method. These findings cover both probabilistic image generation and the perceived realism of enlarged images.
icml-2018-image-transformer-683ae75a4e.tldr: Local self-attention makes Transformer image generation practical and improves reported image likelihood and super-resolution realism.

paragraphs: JointGAN aims to learn the joint distribution of several domains: how their variables behave individually and together. A conditional distribution describes one domain given information about another, while a joint distribution describes their combined behavior. The paper develops an adversarial framework that targets this broader object by learning both conditional relationships and individual domain distributions.

The architecture contains multiple generators and one softmax-based critic, trained together through adversarial learning. The generators learn to sample between domains conditionally and from each domain’s marginal distribution. Training these components together is the mechanism used to support joint distribution matching across the participating domains.

Starting from a simple noise source, the framework can generate samples from one domain, generate conditionally when some variables are observed, or generate complete samples spanning the joint distribution. These capabilities allow several kinds of generation within the same framework. Most presented examples involve two domains, and the authors also include three-domain examples to illustrate a broader setting.
icml-2018-jointgan-multi-domain-joint-di.tldr: JointGAN jointly learns marginal and conditional generators to support sampling from individual domains or their full joint distribution.

paragraphs: This paper studies regularized gradient descent for learning shallow neural networks. Its framework includes several ways to constrain a model, such as sharing weights, encouraging sparsity for pruning, and imposing low-rank structure. These restrictions offer different routes toward compact networks while fitting within a common analysis of learning and optimization.

The authors introduce covering dimension as a measure of the complexity of the permitted parameter set. This provides a way to relate a constraint’s structure to generalization and the amount of data needed for learning. The analysis therefore looks beyond the network’s raw parameter count to the complexity that remains after regularization.

The paper shows that the proposed algorithms have well-behaved local dynamics, including linear convergence, once the amount of data exceeds the covering dimension. Its results establish that near-optimal sample complexity is sufficient for efficient learning in the studied setting. The local nature of the convergence result matters: the conclusion concerns behavior near a solution, and the overall framework focuses on shallow networks.
icml-2018-learning-compact-neural-networ.tldr: For shallow networks, structured regularization links effective model complexity to sufficient data and efficient local convergence.

paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders learn representations by reconstructing inputs in the presence of noise. This paper asks how that noise changes the course of learning. By restricting the theoretical study to linear denoising autoencoders, the authors derive analytic expressions that exactly describe their learning dynamics, making the influence of noise directly accessible to analysis.

The theory shows that appropriately tuned noise allows the model to disregard low-variance directions in the inputs during reconstruction learning. A comparison with standard regularized autoencoders finds that noise produces a regularization effect similar to weight decay, but with faster training dynamics. The tuning qualification matters: the beneficial behavior is associated with suitable noise settings.

The authors test their predictions with simulations and experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Their theoretical predictions approximate learning dynamics on real-world data and qualitatively agree with observations in nonlinear denoising autoencoders. This separates the exact result for linear models from the broader empirical relevance: the nonlinear agreement concerns the pattern of behavior, rather than an exact analytic description.
icml-2018-learning-dynamics-of-linear-de.tldr: Exact linear-autoencoder dynamics explain how tuned noise regularizes learning, with qualitative agreement observed in nonlinear models.

paragraphs: A data distribution reflects the processes that generated its observations. This paper explores whether learning those processes as separate mechanisms can produce components that remain useful beyond one particular distribution. Its focus is on recovering inverse mechanisms from transformed data: operations that map examples back toward a reference distribution.

The proposed unsupervised algorithm uses multiple experts that compete for the transformed examples. Competition drives specialization, with each expert learning to reverse transformations for a subset of the data. This provides a way to divide the recovery problem among distinct learned mechanisms without requiring supervised assignments of examples to experts.

Experiments on image data show each expert learning a mapping back to the reference distribution, and the learned mechanisms generalize to novel domains. These findings support the idea that a transformation mechanism can be useful outside the particular data on which it was learned. The authors discuss how this modular view connects to transfer learning and generative modeling, where reusable components may help organize what a model learns.
icml-2018-learning-independent-causal-me.tldr: Competing unsupervised experts learn specialized inverse transformations that generalize to new image domains.

paragraphs: This paper addresses prediction for processes that vary across both space and time, with observations arriving as a stream. The central challenge is that temporal patterns can differ between spatial regions. A model must therefore represent local differences in repeating behavior while accommodating a training set that grows one observation at a time.

The authors develop a localized spatio-temporal covariance model that captures spatially varying temporal periodicities. Covariance represents relationships among observations, so this formulation places regional differences directly into the model’s account of dependence. They learn its parameters through covariance fitting, obtaining a predictor that can be updated sequentially whenever a new data point arrives.

The method is evaluated on synthetic data and real climate observations. The reported results demonstrate accurate prediction of values missing across spatial regions over time. These findings connect the model’s two main features: its representation of local temporal patterns and its ability to incorporate new observations into an evolving predictor.
icml-2018-learning-localized-spatio-temp.tldr: A sequentially updated covariance model captures region-specific temporal cycles and predicts missing spatio-temporal data.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can be slow because the number of possible combined outputs grows combinatorially. This paper seeks to accelerate a trained structured classifier while preserving its accuracy. The original classifier is treated as a black box, and an additional classifier learns to imitate its behavior through a learning-to-search approach.

As the original model processes more examples, the additional model becomes a learned search heuristic. It guides inference toward promising parts of the output space, reducing the work required to locate useful predictions. The authors also establish a mistake bound and identify particular inference situations in which this speedup classifier can make correct judgments without accessing input features.

The method is evaluated on entity and relation extraction. In those experiments, the learned speedup classifier is faster even than greedy search, with no loss of accuracy. The result shows that information acquired from a classifier’s prediction behavior can help organize subsequent search efficiently, making inference itself a target for learning.
icml-2018-learning-to-speed-up-structure.tldr: A classifier trained to imitate structured prediction learns search guidance that improves inference speed without accuracy loss in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes what happens near a solution when using proximal variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods, concentrating on SAGA and Prox-SVRG. The central assumption is that the nonsmooth part of the objective is partly smooth relative to a smooth manifold. This gives the problem a locally smooth structure that the algorithms can eventually discover.

The authors provide a unified account with two stages. First, the sequence of iterates identifies the relevant smooth manifold after finitely many iterations. Then it enters a local regime of linear convergence. The result explains how an optimization problem containing a nonsmooth component can still exhibit predictable, faster local behavior under the stated structural assumption.

The analysis also motivates acceleration after this structure becomes available. Possibilities include adapting algorithm settings to better local parameters and applying higher-order deterministic or stochastic methods that can achieve superlinear convergence. Examples from machine learning demonstrate the results. These acceleration possibilities build on the local analysis, rather than asserting that the original methods always converge superlinearly.
icml-2018-local-convergence-properties-o.tldr: Under partial smoothness, SAGA and Prox-SVRG identify a smooth manifold and then converge locally at a linear rate.

paragraphs: A neural classifier combines a learned feature transformation with a final decision rule. This paper focuses on that decision rule and asks how its design can improve resistance to adversarial examples. The authors introduce a Max-Mahalanobis distribution and establish a theoretical result: if classifier inputs follow that distribution, linear discriminant analysis has the best adversarial robustness.

The proposed MM-LDA network turns this conditional result into an architectural objective. It explicitly maps a complicated input distribution toward a Max-Mahalanobis distribution in the latent feature space, then applies linear discriminant analysis to classify those features. The feature representation and final classifier are therefore designed around the same distributional target.

The reported results show significantly greater robustness to adversarial attacks and better performance in class-biased classification. These findings support attention to the classifier component when designing robust neural networks. The theoretical optimum remains tied to its distributional condition, while the network’s practical value is demonstrated through the reported robustness and classification results.
icml-2018-max-mahalanobis-linear-discrim.tldr: MM-LDA shapes learned features around a distribution with a conditional robustness guarantee for its final classifier.

paragraphs: This paper examines why gradients can become unreliable in model-based reinforcement learning. The authors’ experiments suggest that long chains of nonlinear computations may behave in a chaos-like way. Gradients can grow large while their directions become essentially random, making the problem more fundamental than numerical magnitude alone.

The study finds that reparameterization gradients suffer from this behavior, whereas likelihood ratio gradients are robust to it. These observations motivate PIPPS, a framework for model-based policy search that supports almost arbitrary models and policies. The authors report that this flexibility is compatible with performance matching earlier data-efficient learning algorithms.

They also introduce total propagation, which combines estimators across different pathwise derivative depths in a single backward pass. It automatically assigns greater weight to estimators with lower variance. The authors report improvements over reparameterization gradients of up to a factor of one million in some cases. This is a conditional result, with the contribution centered on adapting the gradient estimate to its reliability.
icml-2018-pipps-flexible-model-based-pol.tldr: PIPPS addresses unreliable gradients in nonlinear model-based policy search by combining gradient estimators according to their variance.

paragraphs: Controlling a system described by a partial differential equation can require many continuous action values spread across space. Those action dimensions have spatial relationships, making their structure relevant to learning. This paper develops a reinforcement learning approach that explicitly uses these relationships when dealing with high-dimensional control actions.

The authors introduce action descriptors to encode regularities among the spatially extended action dimensions. They incorporate this representation into deep deterministic policy gradient. Theoretical evidence suggests that exploiting such regularity can improve sample efficiency compared with a conventional approach that treats each action dimension separately. The claim is about a possible benefit supported by the analysis, rather than an unconditional guarantee.

Experiments cover two PDE control problems with continuous action spaces containing up to 256 dimensions. The results show an advantage over the conventional approach. Together, the analysis and experiments support representing the organization of the action space as part of the learning problem, so the agent can use spatial relationships when learning control.
icml-2018-reinforcement-learning-with-fu.tldr: Action descriptors help reinforcement learning exploit spatial structure in high-dimensional continuous control of PDE systems.

paragraphs: Program synthesis seeks a source-code program that exactly maps supplied inputs to their outputs. A common approach turns each example into a constraint and asks a solver to find a satisfying program. This becomes expensive when many examples are included, even though a small, carefully selected set can be effective.

The paper proposes an iterative method for constructing a compact, representative subset. A neural network estimates the probability of each unselected example conditional on the examples already chosen. The algorithm then adds the least probable example. This selection rule uses the current subset to identify which remaining example is least anticipated and should be included next.

The authors empirically assess how representative the resulting subsets are and demonstrate significant improvements in synthesis time and stability. The contribution addresses which constraints to present to the solver, linking learned example selection to the cost of exact program construction. The reported gains show that selecting informative examples can make the constraint-solving stage more manageable.
icml-2018-selecting-representative-examp.tldr: A neural selection method builds small representative example sets that improve program synthesis time and stability.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn a decision-making policy from sampled experience. This paper introduces SVRPG, which adapts stochastic variance reduction to policy gradient learning in Markov decision processes. The aim is to bring a successful optimization idea from supervised learning into a setting where the sampling process changes as the policy changes.

That adaptation must address three difficulties: the objective is nonconcave, full gradients can only be approximated, and the data distribution is nonstationary. SVRPG uses importance weights to preserve an unbiased gradient estimate despite the sampling issue. This makes the changing relationship between the policy and its collected experience part of the algorithm’s design.

Under standard assumptions on the Markov decision process, the authors establish convergence guarantees, including a linear convergence rate when batch sizes increase. The increasing-batch condition is part of that rate claim. They also propose practical variants and evaluate them empirically on continuous decision processes, connecting the theoretical algorithm to implementations suited to policy learning.
icml-2018-stochastic-variance-reduced-po.tldr: SVRPG adapts variance reduction to policy learning with importance weighting and proves conditional convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for the empirical success of an adversarial image-to-image translation model. Such a model transforms images between settings, and its observed behavior had lacked a solid account of the underlying mechanism. The authors reformulate the model geometrically to analyze how it operates.

The geometric perspective provides an interpretation of several previously unclear phenomena in the model’s experiments. This makes the reformulation useful as an explanatory tool: it connects aspects of observed behavior with the model’s structure. The paper’s emphasis is on understanding an existing translation framework and extracting consequences from that understanding.

The authors also broaden the definition of generalization for generative adversarial networks and derive a condition for controlling the translation model’s generalization capability. They use that condition to develop practical suggestions for model design and dataset construction. The result links theory to decisions about both the model and its training data, offering guidance for subsequent empirical work within the analyzed framework.
icml-2018-theoretical-analysis-of-image-.tldr: A geometric analysis explains observed adversarial image-translation behavior and yields a condition guiding generalization, model design, and data construction.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often divides interaction into episodes that end after a fixed time. This paper distinguishes two meanings of that cutoff: the agent may be solving a task whose objective truly ends then, or it may be learning an ongoing task using temporary episodes to diversify experience. The distinction changes how training should handle episode endings.

For a genuinely time-limited task, the authors argue that remaining time belongs in the agent’s input. Otherwise, situations that require different decisions can appear identical, violating the Markov property. For an ongoing task interrupted only for training, they argue that learning should bootstrap from the final state’s value, retaining the value of continuation beyond the artificial cutoff.

The paper explains how mishandling these cases can cause state aliasing, invalidate experience replay, and contribute to unstable training or suboptimal policies. Experiments demonstrate improvements in performance and stability for existing algorithms, including leading results on several control tasks. The practical lesson is to make learning updates reflect what an episode ending actually means for the task.
icml-2018-time-limits-in-reinforcement-l.tldr: Reinforcement learning should encode remaining time for true deadlines and bootstrap across cutoffs used only during training.

paragraphs: Tree edit distance compares structured objects through the costs of inserting, deleting, or replacing nodes. Learning those costs can improve classification by making same-class trees closer and different-class trees farther apart. However, directly learned costs may violate metric axioms, be difficult to interpret, or generalize poorly. This paper proposes an indirect way to learn the distance.

Embedding edit distance learning, or BEDL, represents tree nodes as vectors and uses Euclidean distances between them to support class discrimination. Training pulls trees closer to representative trees from their own class and pushes them away from representatives of other classes. The learned vector representation thus determines how local node differences contribute to comparisons between whole trees.

The authors report improvements over leading tree metric learning methods on six benchmark datasets. The examples span computer science, biomedical data, and natural language processing, including a dataset with more than 300,000 nodes. These results support learning the geometry of node symbols as a useful route to improving distances between structured objects.
icml-2018-tree-edit-distance-learning-vi.tldr: BEDL learns vector embeddings for tree symbols to improve class-sensitive edit distances, with gains on six benchmarks.
